T0A01.why: A 12-volt battery won't shock you through dry skin, but it can deliver huge currents. Shorting its terminals, for example with a wrench or wire, can cause burns, fire or even an explosion.

T0A02.why: All of these: current through the body can burn tissue by heating it, disrupt the electrical signals of cells (including the heart), and cause involuntary muscle contractions.

T0A03.why: In US AC wiring, black is the hot (line) conductor, white is neutral, and green or bare is the equipment ground.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 4: Introduction to Electrical Conductors, Wiring Techniques, and Schematic Reading (NAVEDTRA 14176)
src.quote: The other side of the input is called the "line," or hot side, and is color coded "black".

T0A04.why: A fuse removes power when there's an overload: it melts and opens the circuit before the wiring overheats.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 3: Introduction to Circuit Protection, Control, and Measurement (NAVEDTRA 14175)
src.quote: The wire was smaller than the conductor it was protecting and, therefore, would melt before the conductor it was protecting was harmed.

T0A05.why: A 20-amp fuse in place of a 5-amp one would let four times the intended current flow before blowing, which can overheat wiring and start a fire. Always replace a fuse with the same rating.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 3: Introduction to Circuit Protection, Control, and Measurement (NAVEDTRA 14175)
src.quote: Never use a fuse with a higher current rating, a lower voltage rating, or a slower time delay rating than the specified fuse.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 3: Introduction to Circuit Protection, Control, and Measurement (NAVEDTRA 14175)
src.quote: The heat in the wire can char and burn the insulation of the wire

T0A06.why: All of these guard against shock: three-wire grounded cords and plugs, a common safety ground for station equipment, and discharging high-voltage capacitors before working inside equipment.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 4: Introduction to Electrical Conductors, Wiring Techniques, and Schematic Reading (NAVEDTRA 14176)
src.quote: Always discharge the high voltage from components or terminals by using a safety probe.

T0A07.why: Lightning arresters belong on a grounded entry panel where the feed lines come into the building, so surges go to ground outside before reaching your equipment.

T0A08.why: A fuse or breaker goes in series with the hot conductor only, so it cuts off the live side. The neutral shouldn't be fused.

T0A09.why: All ground rods and earth connections should be bonded together with heavy wire or strap, so they stay at the same potential and lightning or fault current can't flow between them through your equipment.

T0A10.why: Charging or discharging an unprotected battery too fast can make it overheat or give off gas, which can be dangerous.

T0A11.why: Filter capacitors can hold a dangerous charge after the power is turned off. Discharge them safely before touching anything inside.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 4: Introduction to Electrical Conductors, Wiring Techniques, and Schematic Reading (NAVEDTRA 14176)
src.quote: Always discharge the high voltage from components or terminals by using a safety probe.

T0A12.why: For high voltages, make sure the voltmeter and its test leads are rated for the voltage you're measuring.

T0B01.why: Lightning ground wires should be short and direct, without sharp bends, so the surge takes the easy path to ground.

T0B02.why: All of these: get proper training in tower climbing, wear an approved climbing harness, and stay tied off to the tower at all times.

T0B03.why: Never climb a tower without a helper or observer on the ground.

T0B04.why: Look for overhead power lines and stay well clear of them. Contact with power lines is one of the deadliest antenna-installation hazards.

T0B05.why: A safety wire through a turnbuckle keeps it from loosening (unscrewing) due to vibration.

T0B06.why: Place the antenna so that if it falls, no part of it can come within 10 feet of power wires.

T0B07.why: Never climb a crank-up tower unless it's fully retracted or mechanical safety locks are in place. The cables or mechanism could fail and drop the sections.

T0B08.why: Use a separate eight-foot ground rod for each tower leg, bonded to the tower and to each other.

T0B09.why: Utility poles carry high-voltage lines, so an antenna mounted on one could contact them. (It isn't allowed anyway without the utility's permission.)

T0B10.why: Avoid sharp bends in lightning grounding conductors: a lightning surge has very fast-changing current, and sharp bends add impedance and can make it jump off the conductor.

T0B11.why: Grounding requirements for towers and antennas are set by local electrical codes (typically based on the National Electrical Code), not by Part 97.

T0C01.why: Radio signals are non-ionizing radiation: they don't have enough energy per photon to knock electrons off atoms or damage DNA.

src.cite: National Cancer Institute, Cell phones and cancer risk fact sheet
src.quote: These frequencies all fall in the nonionizing range of the spectrum, which is low frequency and low energy. The energy is too low to damage DNA.

T0C02.why: The exposure limit is lowest (strictest) from 30 to 300 MHz, where the body absorbs RF most efficiently: 0.2 mW/cm² for the general public. Of the choices, 50 MHz falls in that range. At 3.5 MHz the limit is about 14.7 mW/cm², at 440 MHz about 0.29, and at 1296 MHz about 0.86.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Evaluating Compliance with FCC Guidelines for Human Exposure to Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields
src.quote: whole-body absorption of RF energy by human beings is most efficient.

T0C03.why: Exposure limits are averaged over time. Transmitting only half the time (50% duty cycle) halves the average exposure, so the allowable power density during transmission doubles.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Supplement B (amateur radio stations)
src.quote: during any given six-minute period an amateur or a worker could be exposed to two times the applicable power density limit for three minutes as long as he or she were not exposed at all for the preceding or following three minutes.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Supplement B (amateur radio stations)
src.quote: The concept of power averaging includes both on and off times, and the “duty factor” of the transmitting mode being used.

T0C04.why: All of these: exposure depends on the frequency and power, the distance from the antenna, and the antenna's radiation pattern.

T0C05.why: Limits vary with frequency because the human body absorbs RF energy more efficiently at some frequencies than at others.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Evaluating Compliance with FCC Guidelines for Human Exposure to Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields
src.quote: absorbs RF energy at some frequencies more efficiently than at others.

T0C06.why: All of these are acceptable: calculations using OET Bulletin 65, computer modeling, or measurements with calibrated equipment.

src.quote: it may be necessary for the licensee to calculate the fields that are present by means of equations from this supplement, Bulletin 65, computer modelling, or direct measurements.

T0C07.why: Touching an antenna while it's transmitting can cause an RF burn to the skin.

T0C08.why: Moving antennas farther from people reduces RF exposure. Moving the transmitter alone doesn't help unless the antenna moves too, because the antenna does the radiating. Increasing the duty cycle would make exposure worse.

T0C09.why: Re-evaluate your station whenever you change something in the transmitter or antenna system, since changes can affect exposure.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Supplement B (amateur radio stations)
src.quote: When completed, this worksheet may be retained in the station records so that if and when the setup is changed, it may more easily be re-evaluated.

T0C10.why: Duty cycle matters because exposure limits are based on average exposure over time, and duty cycle sets the average.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Supplement B (amateur radio stations)
src.quote: The concept of power averaging includes both on and off times, and the “duty factor” of the transmitting mode being used.

T0C11.why: Duty cycle is the percentage of time the transmitter is actually transmitting during the averaging period.

src.quote: The concept of power averaging includes both on and off times, and the “duty factor” of the transmitting mode being used.

src.cite: ARRL Technical Information Service, Repeaters: what are they and how to use them

T2B02.why: CTCSS (continuous tone-coded squelch system, also called PL) sends a steady sub-audible tone with your voice. A receiver or repeater set to that tone opens its squelch only when it hears it.

src.cite: ARRL Technical Information Service, Repeaters: what are they and how to use them

T2B14.why: A talkgroup is a DMR identifier that sorts traffic into groups. Your radio plays only the talkgroups it's set for, so you aren't bothered by other traffic.

T3A01.why: Signals often arrive both directly and reflected off buildings and the ground. Where the paths arrive in phase they add, and where out of phase they cancel. Strong and weak spots are about half a wavelength apart, roughly 3 feet on 2 meters, so moving the antenna a few feet can change the signal a lot.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R P.1406-2, Propagation effects relating to terrestrial land mobile and broadcasting services in the VHF and UHF bands
src.quote: On a scale of a few wavelengths, signal variability is determined by multipath effects.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Radio waves that are received in phase reinforce each other and produce a stronger signal at the receiving site. Conversely, those that are received out of phase produce a weak or fading signal.

T3A02.why: Leaves, branches and trees weaken (attenuate) UHF and microwave signals, absorbing and scattering their energy. Weak signals passing through foliage may become unreadable.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R P.833-10, Attenuation in vegetation
src.quote: Attenuation in vegetation can be important in some circumstances, for both terrestrial and Earth-space systems.

T3A03.why: By convention, VHF and UHF weak-signal operators (long-distance CW and SSB) use horizontal polarization, so their antennas match each other. FM and repeater stations mostly use vertical.

T3A04.why: Over a direct (line-of-sight) path the polarization doesn't change much, so a vertical antenna receiving a horizontal signal, or the reverse, picks up much less of it. The received signal is much weaker.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: For maximum absorption of energy from the electromagnetic fields, the receiving antenna must be located in the plane of polarization.

T3A05.why: If the direct path is blocked, try aiming your directional antenna at something that reflects the signal toward the repeater, such as a large building or hillside. VHF and UHF signals reflect well off large objects.

T3A06.why: "Picket fencing" is the rapid flutter you hear on a mobile VHF/UHF signal as the vehicle moves through the pattern of reinforcing and cancelling multipath signals, like running a stick along a picket fence.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R P.1406-2, Propagation effects relating to terrestrial land mobile and broadcasting services in the VHF and UHF bands
src.quote: On a scale of a few wavelengths, signal variability is determined by multipath effects.

T3A07.why: Rain, and other precipitation, absorbs and scatters microwave signals, so range at microwave frequencies drops in wet weather. Wind, air pressure and cold don't have this effect.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: For example, rain has a pronounced effect on waves at microwave frequencies.

T3A08.why: Ionospheric signals often reach you by more than one path (different hops or layers). As the ionosphere shifts, these arrive randomly in and out of phase, so the combined signal fades irregularly.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Usually, however, fading on ionospheric circuits is mainly a result of multipath propagation.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Radio waves that are received in phase reinforce each other and produce a stronger signal at the receiving site. Conversely, those that are received out of phase produce a weak or fading signal.

T3A09.why: The ionosphere changes the polarization of signals passing through it, so by the time they arrive they're elliptically polarized: they have both vertical and horizontal components. Either a vertical or a horizontal antenna can receive them, and the transmitting and receiving antennas don't have to match.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: When a radio wave is refracted by the ionosphere or reflected from the Earth's surface, random changes in the polarization of the wave may occur.

T3A10.why: With multipath, copies of the signal arrive at slightly different times and with different phases, smearing and distorting the data. That makes errors more likely.

src.cite: Recommendation ITU-R P.1406-2, Propagation effects relating to terrestrial land mobile and broadcasting services in the VHF and UHF bands
src.quote: Many types of radio system, particularly those using digital techniques, are sensitive to multipath propagation introduced to the signal by the path characteristics.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This fading causes severe distortion of the signal

T3A11.why: The ionosphere, an upper layer of the atmosphere ionized by the Sun, bends (refracts) HF signals back to Earth, allowing long-distance contacts. The troposphere and stratosphere lie below it.

src.cite: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Ionosphere
src.quote: the ionosphere is important because it reflects and modifies radio waves used for communication and navigation.

T3A12.why: Fog and rain have little effect on 10- and 6-meter signals. Precipitation only absorbs much at much higher, microwave, frequencies.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: with decreases in frequency, precipitation has little attenuation effect.

T3B01.why: A radio wave's electric and magnetic fields are at right angles to each other (and both are at right angles to the direction of travel).

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: it is easier to picture electromagnetic radiation in space as horizontal and vertical lines of force oriented at right angles to each other.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: These lines of force are made up of an electric field (E) and a magnetic field (H), which together make up the electromagnetic field in space.

T3B02.why: Polarization is defined by the orientation of the electric (E) field: vertical if the E field is vertical, horizontal if it's horizontal.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Normally, the plane of polarization of a radio wave is the plane in which the E field propagates with respect to the Earth.

T3B03.why: A radio wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field traveling together.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: An electromagnetic wave consists of two primary components—an ELECTRIC FIELD and a MAGNETIC FIELD.

T3B04.why: In free space, radio waves travel at the speed of light: they are electromagnetic waves, just like light.

src.cite: FCC OET Bulletin 65, Evaluating Compliance with FCC Guidelines for Human Exposure to Radiofrequency Electromagnetic Fields
src.quote: In free space the velocity of an electromagnetic wave is equal to the speed of light

T3B05.why: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related: as frequency goes up, wavelength gets shorter.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This illustrates the principle that the HIGHER THE FREQUENCY, the SHORTER THE WAVELENGTH.

T3B06.why: Since radio waves travel about 300,000,000 meters per second, wavelength in meters is about 300 divided by the frequency in megahertz. For example, 146 MHz is about 2 meters.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: the wavelength divided into 300 yields the frequency in megahertz.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Wavelength-to-frequency conversions of radio waves are really quite simple because wavelength and frequency are reciprocals

T3B07.why: Amateur bands are commonly named by their approximate wavelength, such as 2 meters for 144–148 MHz or 70 centimeters for 420–450 MHz. The FCC's own band tables use these names.

src.quote: Wavelength band ITU Region 1 ITU Region 2 ITU Region 3

T3C01.why: UHF frequencies are far above the highest frequency the ionosphere can bend back to Earth, so they pass through it into space. Without ionospheric skip, UHF signals rarely go much beyond the radio horizon.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Radio waves transmitted at frequencies higher than the critical frequency of a given layer will pass through the layer and be lost in space

T3C02.why: Long-distance contacts by ionospheric skip are routine on HF, but much rarer on VHF and above, where frequencies are usually too high for the ionosphere to return.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The F2 layer is the most important layer for long distance hf communications. It is a very variable layer and its height and density change with time of day, season, and sunspot activity.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Radio waves transmitted at frequencies higher than the critical frequency of a given layer will pass through the layer and be lost in space

T3C03.why: VHF signals scattered by the aurora flutter very rapidly, giving them a distinctive raspy, hissing or growling sound. Phone signals are badly garbled; slow CW gets through best. In the Northern Hemisphere, contacts are made by pointing antennas north, toward the aurora.

src.cite: G. Lange-Hesse, VHF bistatic aurora communications (NASA Technical Reports Server)
src.quote: An aurorally-propagate v.h.f. signal has a characteristic growl or hiss due to a fast fading

src.cite: G. Lange-Hesse, VHF bistatic aurora communications (NASA Technical Reports Server)
src.quote: usually obtained when both stations point their directional antennas northward towards the aurora

T3C04.why: Sporadic E, patches of unusually dense ionization in the E region, can reflect much higher frequencies than the normal ionosphere. It brings occasional strong signals from beyond the horizon on 10, 6 and sometimes 2 meters.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Irregular cloud-like patches of unusually high ionization, called sporadic E, often form at heights near the normal E layer.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This condition may permit the long distance transmission of signals at unusually high frequencies.

T3C05.why: Radio waves bend (diffract) around the sharp edge of an obstruction, such as a ridge or building. Knife-edge diffraction lets some signal reach stations behind it.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: DIFFRACTION is the bending of the wave path when the waves meet an obstruction.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: This change makes it possible to receive energy around the edges of an obstacle

T3C06.why: Tropospheric ducting traps VHF and UHF signals in layers of the lower atmosphere, regularly carrying them a few hundred miles (about 300) beyond the normal horizon.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: vhf and uhf transmissions may be propagated far beyond normal line-of-sight distances.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)

T8D06.why: PSK stands for phase shift keying.

T8D07.why: DMR uses time-division multiplexing to carry two digital voice signals (two time slots) on one 12.5 kHz repeater channel.

T8D08.why: Packet radio (AX.25) frames include a header with the destination and source call signs and a checksum to detect errors, and connected-mode packet automatically re-sends frames with errors (ARQ).

T8D09.why: CW (continuous wave) is another name for Morse code sent by turning a carrier on and off.

T8D10.why: WSJT-X supports all of these: EME (moonbounce), meteor scatter (MSK144), and weak-signal propagation beacons (WSPR).

T8D12.why: An amateur mesh network (such as AREDN) uses commercial Wi-Fi equipment running modified firmware on amateur frequencies to build a data network.

T9A01.why: A beam antenna concentrates its signal in one direction (and hears best from that direction), like a Yagi.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: The ratio between the amount of energy propagated in these directions compared to the energy that would be propagated if the antenna were not directional is known as its gain.

T9A02.why: Loading means changing an antenna's electrical length, for example adding inductors (loading coils) so a physically short antenna acts electrically longer.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: To change the electrical length, you can insert either an inductor or a capacitor in series with the antenna.

T9A03.why: An antenna's polarization is described by the orientation of its electric field: vertical or horizontal.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Normally, the plane of polarization of a radio wave is the plane in which the E field propagates with respect to the Earth.

T9A04.why: A short flexible "rubber duck" antenna is much shorter than a quarter wavelength and relies on loading. It radiates less of the power fed to it (low efficiency) than a full-size quarter-wave antenna.

T9A05.why: Shortening a dipole raises its resonant frequency, because resonant length is inversely related to frequency.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: If the antenna is too short for the wavelength being used, it is resonant at a higher frequency than that at which it is being excited.

T9A06.why: Of these, a Yagi (a beam with parasitic director and reflector elements) has the most gain. Verticals radiate all around, and an isotropic antenna is the zero-gain reference.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: Parasitic arrays represent another method of achieving high antenna gains.

T9A07.why: A car's metal body shields radio signals, so a handheld used inside, with no outside antenna, gets out and hears much less.

T9A08.why: A quarter wavelength at 146 MHz is about 19 inches. Using the practical formula, 234 ÷ 146 ≈ 1.6 ft ≈ 19.2 in. So a 19-inch whip is a resonant quarter-wave on 2 meters.

T9A09.why: A 5/8-wavelength vertical concentrates more energy toward the horizon than a 1/4-wave whip, giving it a few dB more gain.

T9A10.why: A half-wave dipole radiates strongest broadside, at right angles to the wire, and weakest off its ends.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: maximum radiation comes from the doublet in a direction perpendicular to the antenna axis.

T9A11.why: Antenna gain is the increase in signal in a particular direction compared with a reference antenna, such as an isotropic radiator or a dipole.

T9B01.why: None of the common coax connectors (PL-259, BNC, Type N) is reliably waterproof on its own outdoors. Seal and tape them all to keep water out of the connector and cable.

T9B02.why: Most amateur coax is 50 ohms, matching the 50-ohm output of typical transceivers.

T9B03.why: Coax is popular because it's easy to use: it can run next to metal or other cables, be buried, or be bent around obstacles with few special precautions. It isn't the lowest-loss, highest-power or cheapest line.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: in a coaxial line no electric or magnetic fields extend outside of the outer conductor.

T9B04.why: An antenna tuner (coupler) matches the antenna system's impedance to the transmitter's output impedance, so the transmitter sees a proper load.

T9B05.why: Coax loss rises as frequency rises, from skin effect in the conductors and from dielectric loss.

src.cite: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (NAVEDTRA 14182)
src.quote: power losses increase with an increase in frequency because of skin effect.

T9B06.why: Type N connectors keep a constant impedance well into the microwave range, so they suit frequencies above 400 MHz. PL-259/SO-239 connectors aren't constant-impedance, so their performance falls off above about 300–400 MHz.

T9B07.why: PL-259 connectors are the standard on HF and VHF equipment. They aren't watertight, aren't for microwaves, and screw on (not bayonet like BNC).

T9B08.why: All of these add loss: water in connectors, high SWR (which increases loss in the line), and each extra connector.

T9B09.why: A loose connection in the antenna or feed line can make SWR jump around erratically as the contact changes.

T9B10.why: RG-213 is thicker than RG-58, so it has lower loss at a given frequency and handles more power.

T9B11.why: Air-insulated hardline has the lowest loss of these: air is an almost perfect dielectric, and the solid outer conductor confines the signal.

facts.text: In US AC wiring, black is the hot (line) wire.
White is the grounded (neutral) wire, and green connects to the equipment frame and ground.
Never replace a fuse with a higher-rated one; excess current can overheat wiring and start a fire.
Discharge high-voltage capacitors before working inside equipment: they hold a charge after power is off.

T0B.intro: Antenna and tower safety: climbing, power lines, guying, and grounding for lightning protection.

facts.text: Never work on high voltage alone; have a safety observer present. (The same goes for tower climbing: never climb without a helper on the ground.)
Always know where power lines are and stay well clear of them.

T0C.intro: RF exposure safety. RF is non-ionizing, but strong fields can heat tissue. The FCC sets exposure limits, and the station licensee must make sure no one is exposed above them.

facts.text: RF is non-ionizing: it lacks the energy to damage DNA, unlike X-rays.
Limits vary with frequency because the body absorbs RF more efficiently at some frequencies.
The general-population limit is lowest, 0.2 mW/cm², from 30 to 300 MHz.
Exposure is averaged over time, so duty cycle matters: at 50% duty, twice the power density is allowed during transmission.
You can evaluate by calculation (OET Bulletin 65), computer modeling, or measurement.
The licensee is responsible and must act if limits could be exceeded.
Keep your evaluation, and re-evaluate whenever you change the station.

T1A.intro: The amateur service is a voluntary, noncommercial radio service regulated in the US by the FCC under Part 97. These questions cover its purpose, a few key definitions, interference, RACES, phonetics, frequency coordinators and beacons.

facts.text: Part 97's purposes include emergency communications, advancing the radio art, building operators' communication and technical skills, training operators and technicians, and international goodwill.
A space station is any amateur station more than 50 km above the Earth's surface.
Frequency coordinators recommend channels for repeater and auxiliary stations. Local amateurs recognize them; the FCC doesn't appoint them.
Willful or malicious interference is prohibited.
A RACES control operator needs an FCC amateur license and certification of enrollment in a civil defense organization.
Phonetics are encouraged, not required, when identifying by voice.
On HF, beacons may run under automatic control only between 28.20 and 28.30 MHz.

T1B.intro: Which frequencies, modes and power levels a Technician may use. Technicians have all amateur bands from 6 meters up, plus limited HF segments: CW on parts of 80, 40 and 15 meters, and CW, data and SSB voice on part of 10 meters.

facts.text: On 80, 40 and 15 meters, Technicians may use CW only.
On 10 meters, data is allowed from 28.0 to 28.3 MHz and phone from 28.3 to 28.5 MHz, where Technicians may use SSB voice.
6 meters is 50–54 MHz and 2 meters is 144–148 MHz in the US.
50.0–50.1 MHz is CW only, because other modes on 6 meters start at 50.1 MHz.
Likewise 144.0–144.1 MHz is CW only, because other modes on 2 meters start at 144.1 MHz.
Where amateurs are secondary, they must not interfere with primary users and must accept interference from them.
Your signal, including its sidebands, must stay inside your band or segment, so don't set your frequency right at the edge.
Technicians are limited to 200 W PEP in their HF segments.
Above 30 MHz the limit is 1500 W PEP, apart from some band-specific limits.
Always use the minimum power needed.

T1C.intro: Licensing rules: which classes are issued, call sign systems, where your license is valid, keeping your contact details current, the license term and renewal, and what you may say to stations in other countries.

facts.text: New licenses are issued only as Technician, General and Amateur Extra.
Any licensee may apply for a vanity call sign. Technicians may choose from Groups C (1-by-3) and D (2-by-3).
A license normally lasts 10 years.
You may apply to renew no sooner than 90 days before expiration.
After expiration there is a 2-year grace period to renew, but you may not transmit until it is renewed.
Your license must show your correct name, mailing address and email address.
If FCC email to you bounces because your address is wrong, your license can be revoked or suspended.
You may transmit as soon as your license grant appears in the FCC's ULS database.
Your FCC license is good aboard any US-documented or US-registered vessel.
Operating on a ship needs the master's approval.
International contacts are limited to matters incidental to amateur radio and remarks of a personal character.

T1D.intro: What amateurs may and may not transmit. The service is noncommercial and two-way: no broadcasting, no business, no codes or ciphers, and no music, with a few narrow exceptions.

facts.text: No contacts with countries whose administration has told the ITU it objects to them.
Broadcasting (transmissions intended for the general public) is prohibited.
Some one-way transmissions are allowed: brief tests and adjustments, telecommand, emergency communications, Morse practice, information bulletins and telemetry.
No messages encoded to obscure their meaning, except special codes used to command a space station.
Control signals for model craft aren't considered codes meant to obscure meaning.
No obscene or indecent language.
No music, except incidental music in authorized retransmissions of manned spacecraft communications.
No pay for operating, with narrow exceptions such as teachers using a station in classroom instruction.
You may occasionally advertise amateur gear for sale or trade, but not on a regular basis.
Model craft control signals don't need on-air identification if the transmitter carries a label with your call sign, name and address.

T1E.intro: Every amateur station needs a control operator when it transmits. The control operator is responsible for the station following the rules, and their license class decides the station's privileges.

facts.text: A station must have a control operator whenever it transmits.
The station licensee designates the control operator and is presumed to be the control operator unless records show otherwise.
When the control operator isn't the licensee, both are equally responsible.
The station operates with the privileges of the control operator's license class.
The control point is where the control operator function is performed.
Local and remote control need the control operator at the control point; any station may be remotely controlled, for example over the internet.
Under automatic control (repeaters, for example) the control operator need not be at the control point.

T1F.intro: Station identification, repeaters, third-party traffic, club stations and FCC inspections.

facts.text: Give your call sign at least every 10 minutes during a communication and at the end of it, even when using tactical calls.
Identify by voice in English, or by CW. Phonetics are encouraged.
Indicators are separated from your call sign by a slant mark or a word that means it, like "stroke", "slant" or "slash".
Third-party communications are messages sent on behalf of another person.
International third-party traffic is allowed only with countries that have an arrangement with the US, apart from emergency or disaster relief traffic.
A repeater retransmits another station on a different channel. Its control operator isn't accountable for rule violations it passes along inadvertently.
A club station license requires a club of at least four people.
The licensee must make the station and its records available whenever an FCC representative asks.

T2A.intro: Everyday operating: picking a frequency, calling and answering, and how repeaters and band plans organize the VHF and UHF bands. None of this is FCC law; it's the shared practice that keeps the bands usable.

facts.text: A band plan is a voluntary agreement on which modes go where within a band, beyond what the FCC rules require.
146.52 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency on 2 meters.
446.00 MHz is the national FM simplex frequency on 70 cm.
Simplex means both stations transmit and receive on the same frequency.
A repeater's input and output are separated by a set amount for each band, called the offset.
Typical offsets are 600 kHz on 2 meters (e.g. output 145.110, input 144.510 MHz).
On 70 cm the typical offset is 5 MHz.
On 1.25 meters it is 1.6 MHz.
To call a station on a repeater, give their call and then yours. To announce you're available, give your call, perhaps with "listening".
Off the repeaters (on HF, for instance), call CQ a few times, say "this is" and your call, then listen. CQ means a general call to all stations.
When answering, give the other station's call first, then "this is" and yours.

T2B.intro: Practical VHF/UHF operating: getting into repeaters with access tones, using the reverse function and simplex, DMR digital voice (talkgroups and color codes), the squelch control, sharing frequencies, and the common Q signals.

facts.text: Many repeaters only respond to signals carrying the right sub-audible CTCSS (PL) tone.
If you can hear a repeater but can't access it, check your offset, CTCSS tone or DCS code.
DTMF (the telephone keypad tones) sends two tones at once for each key, and is used for repeater control and autopatch.
The reverse function lets you listen on the repeater's input. If you can hear the other station there, move to simplex.
DMR radios join a talkgroup by having its ID programmed in; calls to other talkgroups are ignored.
A DMR radio must match the repeater's color code to use it.
No station has exclusive rights to a frequency; stations must cooperate in sharing.
Common Q signals: QRM (interference from other stations), QRN (static), QSB (fading), QSY (change frequency), QRZ (who is calling me?), QTH (location), QSL (receipt acknowledged).

T2C.intro: Public service and emergency communications: RACES and ARES, how nets run, formal message traffic, and what the rules allow in a real emergency.

RACES is an amateur service for civil defense communications.
RACES control operators must be certified as enrolled in a civil defense organization.
ARES is a volunteer group of licensed amateurs registered for public service communications.

In an emergency involving immediate safety of life or property, with normal communications unavailable, a station may use any means of radio communication at its disposal, even outside its normal privileges.
The net control station directs the net. On a directed net, transmit only when net control recognizes you, except to report an emergency.
"Traffic" means formal messages. A radiogram has a preamble (tracking information), address, text and signature.
The check in the preamble is the number of words in the message text.
Spell unusual words with the phonetic alphabet (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie...).
Winlink is a radio email system; your address is your call sign at winlink.org.

T3A.intro: Why signals get stronger, weaker or flutter: radio waves reflect, scatter and get absorbed, and often reach you by more than one path at once. How antennas are oriented (polarization) matters too.

facts.text: Multipath means a signal arriving by more than one route, such as direct and reflected.

Over distances of just a few wavelengths, multipath makes signal strength vary: strong and weak spots are about half a wavelength apart (roughly 3 feet on 2 meters). On a moving vehicle this shows up as rapid flutter, called "picket fencing".
Fading on ionospheric (HF) paths is mainly caused by multipath.
Digital signals are especially sensitive to multipath, which raises error rates.
For best reception, the receiving antenna should match the wave's polarization. Over a direct VHF/UHF path, cross-polarized antennas lose much of the signal.
Signals that pass through the ionosphere come back with random, mixed (elliptical) polarization, so on HF either antenna orientation works.
The ionosphere is the region of the upper atmosphere that bends HF signals back to Earth.
Rain absorbs and scatters signals at microwave frequencies; at HF and low VHF (like 10 and 6 meters) it has little effect.
Trees and foliage weaken VHF, UHF and microwave signals.
Radio waves reflect off large objects, so a blocked path can sometimes be worked by aiming at a reflection.

T3B.intro: The basic physics of radio waves. A radio wave is an electromagnetic wave, an electric field and a magnetic field traveling together at the speed of light. Its frequency and wavelength are tied together by that speed.

facts.text: A radio wave has two parts: an electric field and a magnetic field, at right angles to each other.
Polarization is set by the direction of the electric field.
In free space, all radio waves travel at the speed of light.
That is exactly 299,792,458 meters per second; use 300,000,000 m/s for exam math.
Higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
Wavelength in meters ≈ 300 ÷ frequency in MHz (and frequency in MHz ≈ 300 ÷ wavelength in meters). Example: 300 ÷ 146 ≈ 2.05 m, so 146 MHz is in the 2-meter band.
HF is 3–30 MHz, VHF 30–300 MHz, UHF 300–3000 MHz.
Amateur bands are usually named by approximate wavelength ("2 meters", "70 centimeters"), as in the FCC's own tables.

T3C.intro: How signals get beyond the horizon. VHF and UHF normally travel in straight lines a little past the visible horizon, while HF can skip off the ionosphere around the world. Several special modes let VHF go much farther now and then.

facts.text: The atmosphere bends VHF and UHF waves slightly, so the radio horizon is beyond the straight-line (geometric) horizon.
Engineers model this bending as an Earth 4/3 its real size. Horizon distance grows with the square root of Earth's radius, and √(4/3) ≈ 1.15, so the radio horizon is about 15% farther away.
Waves too high in frequency for an ionospheric layer to bend back pass through it into space. That's why UHF rarely goes beyond the horizon.
The F2 region carries most long-distance HF; it changes with time of day, season and sunspots.
The Sun ionizes the ionosphere, so the daytime side is much more ionized than the night side. 10 meters is best from about dawn to just after sunset.
Near the sunspot maximum, ionization rises enough for F-region skip on 10 and even 6 meters.
Sporadic E: patches of dense ionization in the E region that can reflect unusually high frequencies, bringing occasional strong signals on 10, 6 and 2 meters.
Tropospheric ducting: a temperature inversion (warm air over cool) traps VHF/UHF signals, carrying them hundreds of miles.
Meteor scatter uses ionized meteor trails; it works best around 30–100 MHz, which makes 6 meters the best amateur band for it.
Auroral VHF signals sound raspy or hissing because of rapid fading. In the Northern Hemisphere, point your antenna north toward the aurora.
Knife-edge diffraction: waves bend around a sharp obstruction's edge and reach stations behind it.

T4A.intro: Putting a station together: powering the radio, where meters go, bonding, mobile installation, and the connections needed to run digital modes from a computer.

facts.text: Mobile rigs (and many base radios) run on 13.8 V DC. A 50-watt FM mobile draws about 10 A on transmit, so choose a supply rated a bit higher (12 A or more).
Use short, heavy-gauge DC leads to keep voltage drop low when transmitting.
In a vehicle, connect red to the battery's positive terminal and black directly to its negative terminal.
Battery run time ≈ ampere-hour rating ÷ average current draw. Example: 20 Ah ÷ 2 A ≈ 10 hours.
For digital modes like FT8, connect radio audio to and from the computer's sound input and output, plus a keying (PTT, CAT or VOX) connection.

T4B.intro: The controls on a transceiver: tuning, squelch, scanning, filters, RIT, microphone gain, and setting up digital voice radios (DMR codeplugs and talkgroups), plus identification.

facts.text: Squelch mutes the receiver when no signal is present. Raising it silences noise but can hide weak signals, so open it up to hear a weak station.
Selectivity is a receiver's ability to separate the wanted signal from unwanted ones. Choosing a filter bandwidth that matches the mode (about 2.4 kHz for SSB, narrower for CW) improves it.
AGC (automatic gain control) evens out changes in received signal strength, so you don't have to keep adjusting the volume.
DMR radios use talkgroup IDs: the radio joins only calls to talkgroups it's programmed for. The codeplug is the configuration file that holds these settings.
You must give your call sign at the end of each contact and at least every 10 minutes during it, on any mode.

T5A.intro: The basic quantities of electricity. Voltage is the push, current is the flow of electrons, resistance opposes the flow, and power is how fast energy is used.

facts.text: Voltage (electromotive force, or potential difference) is measured in volts. A difference in voltage is what makes electrons flow.
Current, the flow of electrons, is measured in amperes.
Resistance opposes current (DC, AC or RF) and is measured in ohms.
Power is the rate of using energy, measured in watts.
Metals conduct well because they have many free electrons. Insulators such as glass, rubber and plastic have few.
Direct current flows one way. Alternating current keeps reversing direction.
Frequency is cycles per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

T5B.intro: Unit conversions and decibels. Metric prefixes step by factors of 1000, and decibels express power ratios.

facts.text: Milli = one-thousandth, micro = one-millionth, pico = one-millionth of a millionth.
Decibels compare two powers: dB = 10 × log₁₀(new power ÷ original power). A negative result means a loss.
Rules of thumb: double the power = +3 dB, half = −3 dB, a quarter = −6 dB, 10× = +10 dB.

T5C.intro: Capacitance, inductance and impedance, their units, how unit symbols are written, and calculating DC power.

facts.text: Capacitance stores energy in an electric field and is measured in farads.
Inductance stores energy in a magnetic field and is measured in henrys.
Impedance is the total opposition to AC (resistance and reactance combined), measured in ohms.
Case matters in unit symbols: kHz (small k), MHz (capital M; small m means milli), and Hz with a capital H.
DC power: P = I × E. Example: 13.8 V × 10 A = 138 W; and I = P ÷ E, so 120 W at 12 V draws 10 A.

reading.title: US Navy, NEETS Module 2: Introduction to Alternating Current and Transformers

T5D.intro: Ohm's law ties voltage, current and resistance together. Series and parallel circuits divide current and voltage in different ways.

facts.text: E = I × R. Example: 2 A through 10 Ω gives 20 V.
I = E ÷ R. Example: 120 V across 80 Ω gives 1.5 A.
R = E ÷ I. Example: 90 V and 3 A means 30 Ω.
Series circuit: the same current flows through every component.
Parallel circuit: the same voltage is across every branch.

T6A.intro: Basic components: resistors and potentiometers, capacitors, inductors, switches and batteries.

facts.text: A resistor opposes current. A potentiometer is a variable resistor, often used as a volume control.
A capacitor is two conductive plates separated by an insulator (the dielectric), and stores energy in an electric field.
An inductor is usually a coil of wire, and stores energy in a magnetic field.
SPST switches turn one circuit on or off. SPDT switches connect one circuit to either of two others.
Nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion, nickel-cadmium and lead-acid batteries are rechargeable.
Carbon-zinc and alkaline cells are single-use.

reading.title: US Navy, NEETS Module 1: Introduction to Matter, Energy, and Direct Current
US EPA, Used household batteries

T6B.intro: Semiconductors: diodes let current flow one way, LEDs give off light, and transistors switch and amplify.

facts.text: A diode passes current in only one direction. Its electrodes are the anode and cathode, and the cathode end is usually marked with a band.
An LED gives off light when forward current flows through it.
A bipolar transistor has three regions, the emitter, base and collector.
A field-effect transistor (FET) has a gate, source and drain.
Gain is output compared with input, as a voltage, current or power ratio. Transistors can provide power gain.

facts.text: A schematic shows electrical connections with standard symbols.

T6D.intro: What components do in circuits: rectifiers, relays, regulators, transformers, indicators, integrated circuits, resonant circuits and shielding.

facts.text: A power supply is typically a transformer, a rectifier, a filter and a regulator.
A transformer changes AC voltage, for example stepping 120 V down.
A rectifier (diode) turns AC into pulsating DC.
A regulator holds the output voltage steady.
A relay is an electrically operated switch.
An integrated circuit puts a complete circuit on one chip.
An inductor plus a capacitor (in series or parallel) makes a resonant, or tuned, circuit.
Shielded cable keeps unwanted signals from coupling into or out of the wire.

reading.title: US Navy, NEETS Module 7: Introduction to Solid-State Devices and Power Supplies (chapter 4)
US Navy, NEETS Module 2: Introduction to Alternating Current and Transformers

T7A.intro: The building blocks of radio equipment: receivers and transmitters, oscillators and mixers, modulation, and add-ons like amplifiers and transverters.

facts.text: Sensitivity is a receiver's ability to pick up weak signals.
Selectivity is its ability to separate the wanted signal from others.
An oscillator generates a signal at a specific frequency; the VFO is the one that sets your operating frequency.
A mixer combines two signals to produce sum and difference frequencies, converting a signal to a new frequency.
Modulation puts information, such as your voice, onto an RF carrier.

reading.title: US Navy, NEETS Module 17: Radio-Frequency Communications Principles
US Navy, NEETS Module 12: Modulation Principles

T7B.intro: Interference and signal problems: overload, spurious emissions, over-deviation and RF feedback, and how to work cooperatively with neighbors.

facts.text: Fundamental overload: a strong signal on its proper frequency can still swamp a nearby receiver that can't reject it.
The cure for overload goes on the affected device, for example a filter at its antenna input.
Spurious emissions (signals off your assigned frequency, including harmonics) are the transmitter operator's responsibility to fix.
If your own TVs and radios work fine while you transmit, the problem is very likely not your station.
For cable TV interference, first check for damaged wiring and loose connectors.
Devices such as consumer electronics must not cause harmful interference.

reading.title: ARRL and CEA, What to do if you have an electronic interference problem
ARRL, Radio Frequency Interference (RFI)

T7C.intro: Feed lines and antennas: SWR, dummy loads, where feed line losses go, and what makes coax fail.

facts.text: SWR 1:1 is a perfect match; anything higher is a mismatch.
A dummy load is a non-reactive resistor that absorbs the transmitter's power, so you can test without radiating.
Power lost in a feed line turns into heat.

reading.title: US Navy, NEETS Module 10: Introduction to Wave Propagation, Transmission Lines, and Antennas (chapter 3)

T7D.intro: Using meters and soldering. Voltmeters go across a part and ammeters go in series. Measure resistance only with the power off. Use rosin-core solder.

facts.text: Voltmeters connect in parallel; ammeters (or a multimeter set to current) connect in series.
A multimeter combines a voltmeter, ammeter and ohmmeter.
An ohmmeter uses its own battery, so remove power from the circuit before measuring resistance.
Never use acid-core solder or acid flux on electronics; use rosin.

T8A.intro: Choosing a mode. SSB is a narrow form of AM, good for weak signals. FM is used for repeaters and packet. Each mode takes up a different amount of spectrum.

facts.text: CW needs only about 100–150 Hz; the FCC's example for 25 words per minute is 100 Hz.
SSB voice is about 3 kHz wide (the FCC's example is 2.7 kHz).
FM voice with ±5 kHz deviation is roughly 10–16 kHz wide.
An analog fast-scan TV signal is about 6 MHz wide.

T8B.intro: Amateur satellites act like repeaters in the sky, usually receiving on one band and transmitting on another. Their motion causes Doppler shift and fading.

facts.text: Tracking programs predict passes from a satellite's Keplerian elements.
Beacons send telemetry about the satellite's health and status.
Because the beacon's power is fixed, it's a good reference for setting your uplink power: aim for a downlink signal about as strong as the beacon.
Mode names give the uplink band, then the downlink band: U/V means a 70 cm uplink and a 2 m downlink.
Doppler shift: frequencies appear higher as the satellite approaches and lower as it leaves.
Most amateur satellites are in low Earth orbit (LEO). (Such orbits take roughly 90–100 minutes.)
Satellites spin and tumble, so their antenna orientation keeps changing and causes spin fading.
Don't overpower the uplink: high-power stations hog the satellite.

reading.title: AMSAT, For Beginners: an amateur radio satellite primer
AMSAT, Station and operating hints

T8C.intro: Operating activities: direction finding (fox hunting), contesting, grid locators, and linking radio to the internet with IRLP, EchoLink and gateways.

facts.text: EchoLink connects licensed amateurs to repeaters and nodes over the internet; you must register and prove you're licensed first.

reading.title: EchoLink, Validation
ARRL, Grid squares

T8D.intro: Digital and non-voice modes: CW, packet and APRS, PSK, DMR, the WSJT-X modes such as FT8, error correction, and amateur mesh networks.

facts.text: WSJT-X is built for communicating with very weak signals.
JT65 was designed for EME (moonbounce).
MSK144 and similar fast modes use brief reflections from meteor trails.
WSPR is used for low-power propagation beacons.
DMR fits two digital voice channels (time slots) onto one 12.5 kHz channel.

reading.title: WSJT-X User Guide, introduction (GitHub mirror)

T9A.intro: Antennas: polarization, gain and beams, resonant length, loading, and the antennas used on handhelds and in cars.

facts.text: Polarization follows the antenna's electric field: a vertical antenna is vertically polarized.
Gain is how much more signal an antenna sends in a particular direction compared with a reference antenna.
Beams such as the Yagi use parasitic elements (a director and a reflector) to get high gain in one direction.
Loading coils make a short antenna electrically longer. A shorter antenna resonates at a higher frequency.
